[[File:Heatmap_of_GCD_Matrix.png|thumb|Heatmap of GCD Matrix]]
In [[mathematics]], a  [[greatest common divisor]] matrix (sometimes abbreviated as '''GCD matrix''') is a [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] that may also be referred to as '''Smith's matrix'''. The study was initiated by H.J.S. Smith (1875). A new inspiration was begun from the paper of Bourque & Ligh (1992). This led to intensive investigations on singularity and divisibility of GCD type matrices. A brief review of papers on GCD type matrices before that time is presented in {{harvtxt|Haukkanen|Wang|Sillanpää|1997}}.

Let <math>S=(x_1, x_2,\ldots, x_n)</math> be a list of positive integers. Then the <math>n\times n</math> matrix <math>(S)</math> having the [[greatest common divisor]] <math>\gcd(x_i, x_j)</math> as its <math>ij</math> entry is referred to as the GCD matrix on <math>S</math>.The [[least common multiple]] (LCM) matrix <math>[S]</math> is defined analogously.{{r|borque-ligh|hong}}

The study of GCD type matrices originates from {{harvtxt|Smith|1875}} who evaluated the determinant of certain GCD and LCM matrices. 
Smith showed among others that the determinant of the <math>n\times n</math> matrix <math>(\gcd(i,j))</math> is <math>\phi(1)\phi(2)\cdots\phi(n)</math>, where <math>\phi</math> is [[Euler's totient function]].{{r|smith}}

== Bourque–Ligh conjecture ==
{{harvtxt|Bourque|Ligh|1992}} conjectured that the LCM matrix on a GCD-closed set <math> S </math> is nonsingular.{{r|borque-ligh}} This conjecture was shown to be false by {{harvtxt|Haukkanen|Wang|Sillanpää|1997}} and subsequently by {{harvtxt|Hong|1999}}.{{r|haukkanen|hong}} A lattice-theoretic approach is provided by {{harvtxt|Korkee|Mattila|Haukkanen|2019}}.{{r|korkee}} 

The [[counterexample]] presented in {{harvtxt|Haukkanen|Wang|Sillanpää|1997}} is <math>S = \{1,2,3,4,5,6, 10,45,180\}</math> and that in {{harvtxt|Hong|1999}} is 
<math>S=\{1,2,3,5,36,230,825,227700\}.</math> A counterexample consisting of odd numbers is <math>S = \{1, 3, 5, 7, 195, 291, 1407, 4025, 1020180525 \}</math>. Its [[Hasse diagram]] is presented on the right below.  

The cube-type structures of these sets with respect to the divisibility relation are explained in {{harvtxt|Korkee|Mattila|Haukkanen|2019}}. [[File:Counterexample.png|thumb|The Hasse diagram of an odd GCD closed set whose LCM matrix is singular]]
== Divisibility ==

Let <math>S=(x_1, x_2,\ldots, x_n)</math> be a factor closed set. 
Then the GCD matrix <math>(S)</math> divides the LCM matrix <math>[S]</math> in the ring of <math>n\times n</math> matrices over the integers, that is there is an integral matrix <math>B</math> such that <math>[S]=B(S)</math>, 
see {{harvtxt|Bourque|Ligh|1992}}. Since the matrices <math>(S)</math> and <math>[S]</math> are symmetric, we have <math>[S]=(S) B^T</math>. Thus, divisibility from the right coincides with that from the left. We may thus use the term divisibility. 

There is in the literature a large number of generalizations and analogues of this basic divisibility result.

== Generalized eigenvalues ==

For <math>S=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}</math>, the generalized eigenvalues of the LCM matrix <math>[S]</math> with respect to the corresponding GCD matrix <math>(S)</math> are the values <math>\lambda</math> satisfying
:<math>
\det([S]-\lambda(S))=0.
</math>
Merikoski, Haukkanen, Sasaki, and Tossavainen compared this problem with the analogous generalized eigenvalue problem for MAX and MIN matrices. They determined the MAX–MIN generalized eigenvalues for every <math>n\geq 1</math> and showed that the corresponding LCM–GCD result holds for <math>n\leq 4</math>, but fails in general for <math>n>4</math>.{{r|merikoski}}

== Matrix norms ==

Some results on matrix norms of GCD type matrices are presented in the literature. 
Two basic results concern the asymptotic behaviour of the <math>\ell_p</math> norm of 
the GCD and LCM matrix on <math>S=\{1, 2,\dots, n\}</math>. {{r|haukkanen-toth}}

  
Given <math>p\in\N^+</math>, the <math>\ell_p</math> norm of an <math>n\times n</math> matrix <math>A</math> is defined as
:<math>
\Vert A\Vert_p
=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n |a_{ij}|^p \right)^{1/p}.
</math>

Let  <math>S=\{1, 2,\dots, n\}</math>. If <math>p\ge 2</math>, then 
:<math>
\Vert (S)\Vert_p=C_p^{1/p} n^{1+(1/p)}+O((n^{(1/p)-p}E_p(n)),
</math>
where 
:<math>
C_p:=\frac{2\zeta(p)-\zeta(p+1)}{(p+1)\zeta(p+1)}
</math>
and <math>E_p(x)=x^p</math> for <math>p>2</math> and <math>E_2(x)=x^2\log x</math>. 
Further,  if <math>p\ge 1</math>, then
:<math>
\Vert [S]\Vert_p=D_p^{1/p} n^{2+(2/p)}+O((n^{(2/p)+1}(\log n)^{2/3}(\log\log n)^{4/3}), 
</math>
where 
:<math> 
D_p:=\frac{\zeta(p+2)}{(p+1)^2\zeta(p)}.
</math>

== Factorizations ==

Let <math>f</math> be an arithmetical function, and let  <math>S=(x_1, x_2,\ldots, x_n)</math> be a set of distinct positive integers. Then the matrix <math>(S)_f=(f(\gcd(x_i, x_j))</math> is referred to as the GCD matrix  on <math>S</math> associated with <math>f</math>.
The LCM matrix <math>[S]_f</math> on <math>S</math> associated with <math>f</math> is defined analogously. 
One may also use the notations  <math>(S)_f=f(S)</math> and <math>[S]_f=f[S]</math>. 

Let <math>S</math> be a GCD-closed set. 
Then
:<math>
(S)_f=E\Delta E^T,
</math>
where <math>E</math> is  the <math>n\times n</math> matrix defined by
:<math>
e_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1 & \mbox{if } x_j\,\mid\, x_i,\\
0 & \mbox{otherwise}
\end{cases}
</math>
and <math>\Delta</math> is the <math>n\times n</math> [[diagonal matrix]],  whose diagonal elements are
:<math>
\delta_i=\sum_{d\mid x_i\atop {d\nmid x_t\atop x_t<x_i}}
(f\star\mu)(d).
</math>
Here <math>\star</math> is the [[Dirichlet convolution]] and <math>\mu</math> is the [[Möbius function]]. 

Further, if <math>f</math> is a [[multiplicative function]] and always nonzero,
then
:<math>
[S]_f=\Lambda E\Delta^\prime E^T\Lambda,
</math>
where <math>\Lambda</math> and <math>\Delta'</math> are the <math>n\times n</math> diagonal matrices,  whose diagonal elements are
<math>\lambda_i=f(x_i)</math> 
and
:<math>
\delta_i^\prime=\sum_{d\vert x_i\atop {d\nmid x_t\atop x_t<x_i}}
(\frac{1}{f}\star\mu)(d).
</math>
If <math>S</math> is factor-closed, then <math>\delta_i=(f\star\mu)(x_i)</math> and 
<math>\delta_i^\prime=(\frac{1}{f}\star\mu)(x_i)</math>.  {{r|haukkanen-toth}}
